passage:
Mentor's note, Friday, first month. Siddharth joined the sales team three weeks ago. I have watched him watch the office. He noticed that the boss's lunch table has the same four people, and that after-work outings are announced by a look, not an email. He asked me quietly, “Is it always like this?” I said every office has a map, and that seeing it clearly is useful. He nodded but stayed tense.

What I did next: I suggested he eat one lunch a week at the boss's table if invited, but also spend time with the operations team, whose work he needs to learn. I told him I'd rather he learn the map and choose than chase it. He booked coffee with Meena from operations.
— Yogesh

qa.q: How many people sit at the boss's lunch table?
qa.a: The same four people sit at the boss's lunch table.

qa.q: What did Siddharth's quiet question, “Is it always like this?”, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Siddharth felt uneasy on noticing who was close to the boss and wondered whether newcomers can belong.

qa.q: What did Yogesh advise Siddharth to do instead of chasing the boss's circle?
qa.a: Yogesh suggested learning the map and choosing where to invest, including time with the operations team.

qa.q: How might the boss see the lunch table?
qa.a: The boss may see it as a comfortable habit of eating with people who have worked together longest, not a deliberate ranking, though a newcomer can read it as one.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a new employee noticing lunch tables and outings that mark who is close to the boss, and choosing where to invest.

passage:
Tuesday. Week three. Things I've worked out without asking: the boss, Kiran, eats at the window table every day with the same four people. After-work chai on Thursdays is for them, and the invitation comes as a glance. On Monday Bhavna from accounts, who sits by the printer and has been here longest, ate alone and nobody minded.

I caught myself planning how to get a window seat. I stopped. Instead I asked Bhavna to explain the invoicing system over lunch, and it turns out she's brilliant and funny. I don't need the window table this month. I need to know how things work.

Maybe I'll be invited someday. We'll see.
— Santosh

qa.q: Where does Kiran eat every day?
qa.a: Kiran eats at the window table every day with the same four people.

qa.q: Why did Santosh stop while planning how to get a window seat?
qa.a: Santosh saw that chasing the table would drain energy and preferred to learn how things work.

qa.q: What choice did Santosh make instead of planning for the window seat?
qa.a: Santosh asked Bhavna to explain the invoicing system over lunch.

qa.q: What might it be like for Bhavna, eating alone until someone sat down?
qa.a: Bhavna may feel overlooked at times, and probably feels pleased and respected that a newcomer asked for advice.

grounding: A new employee sees that lunch tables and after-work chai mark closeness to the boss, and chooses to invest in learning rather than chasing the circle.

passage:
On her first week at the district cooperative bank in the kasba, Nirmala noticed where people drank their evening chai.
The branch manager went to Gopal's stall at five. The same three clerks always went with him. They came back laughing, and the next day they seemed to know things before anyone else. Farzana, who'd been there five years, never went. She had her tea at her desk and still got the tough loan files, because she was good.
Nirmala thought about it on the bus home. She could chase the chai stall. Or she could learn the loan rules like Farzana.
The next week she went to the stall once, said hello, and came back early. Then she asked Farzana to teach her the gold-loan forms.

qa.q: Where did the branch manager go at five?
qa.a: To Gopal's stall.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling as she thought on the bus home?
qa.a: She felt thoughtful and a bit unsure, weighing whether to chase the inner circle or build her skills.

qa.q: Why was Nirmala's choice a balanced one?
qa.a: She showed her face at the stall once without obsessing over it, and invested in learning from Farzana, who was respected for her work.

qa.q: How might Farzana feel when Nirmala asks to learn from her?
qa.a: She might feel pleased and respected, since her skill, not the chai stall, is what Nirmala values.

grounding: Shows a new employee noticing that evening chai marks who is close to the manager, and choosing where to invest without obsessing.

passage:
In his first month at the architecture firm in Sydney, Wei noticed the pattern. The director ate lunch with the same five people on the balcony. On Fridays, those five went to the pub with her, and on Mondays they seemed to have the best projects.
Wei asked Clara, who'd been there three years, about it.
“Oh, the balcony crew,” she laughed. “Yes, it matters a bit. But I've never been on the balcony, and I lead the library project.”
Wei thought about it all weekend. He could try hard to get onto the balcony. Or he could do great work and get to know people slowly.
On Friday he joined the pub once and left early. On Monday he asked Clara if he could help with the library drawings.

qa.q: Where did the director eat lunch?
qa.a: On the balcony with the same five people.

qa.q: How did Wei feel as he thought about it all weekend?
qa.a: He felt thoughtful and a little uncertain, weighing the inner circle against his own work.

qa.q: What does Wei's choice show about handling office inner circles?
qa.a: It shows he can notice the map and join sometimes, while mainly investing in good work and real relationships.

qa.q: How does Clara see the balcony crew?
qa.a: She sees it with light humour; it matters a bit, but she has built her place through her work instead.

grounding: Shows a new employee noticing that lunch and pub outings mark who is close to the boss, and choosing where to invest without obsessing.

passage:
In his second week at the design studio in Gurugram, Pankaj worked out the lunch map. The round table by the window was the boss's: Meera ma'am, the two senior designers and whoever had pitched well that week. The long table near the pantry was the juniors'. Friday outings worked the same way; the window table went, and the rest saw the photos on Monday.
Nitin, who'd joined a year earlier, said, "Don't waste energy trying to get onto that table. I did. Spent three months laughing at jokes I didn't find funny."
Pankaj noticed Nitin wasn't bitter. He just ate at the long table and got his work reviewed early. So Pankaj did the same: lunch with juniors he actually liked, and one short check-in with Meera ma'am every Thursday about his drafts.
He didn't obsess over the window table. But he knew exactly where it was.

qa.q: Where was Meera ma'am's lunch table?
qa.a: The round table by the window.

qa.q: How does Pankaj seem to feel once he understands the lunch map?
qa.a: Pankaj seems calm and clear-headed rather than anxious, aware of the inner circle without craving a seat there.

qa.q: What did Pankaj choose to invest in, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Real friendships at the long table and a steady Thursday check-in about his work, which builds trust with the boss through results.

qa.q: What was chasing the window table like for Nitin?
qa.a: Nitin felt tired and fake, spending three months laughing at jokes he didn't enjoy, and is more at ease now.

grounding: Shows a new employee noticing how lunch tables and outings mark closeness to the boss, and choosing where to invest without obsessing over it.
